title: Judges 19:22–30
context: Wicked men of Gibeah surround the house and demand the Levite; the host offers his daughter and the concubine instead, and the Levite forces his concubine out to them. She is raped and abused through the night, falls at the door by morning, and is found there by the Levite, who later cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel. The scene deliberately echoes Genesis 19, showing an Israelite town acting like Sodom, and the narrator reports these horrors without approving them. The text names this evil plainly, and so should readers: the woman is a victim of grievous violence, and neither the men of Gibeah, nor the host, nor the Levite is excused. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly agree that this passage exposes the depth of human sin when God’s people abandon his ways, calls for grief and justice, and points to the need for righteous rule; no doctrinal dispute divides them here.

verses.text: As they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, certain wicked fellows, surrounded the house, beating at the door; and they spoke to the master of the house, the old man, saying, “Bring out the man who came into your house, that we can have sex with him!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the men of the city, called wicked fellows, surrounding the house and demanding the Levite in order to abuse him. The narrator names their intent plainly as wickedness and violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the deliberate echo of Genesis 19:4, showing an Israelite town behaving like Sodom. Both traditions commonly read the verse as revealing the depth of corruption in Gibeah, an assault on the guest that violates every law of hospitality and decency.

verses.text: The man, the master of the house, went out to them, and said to them, “No, my brothers, please don’t act so wickedly; since this man has come into my house, don’t do this folly.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the host calls the demand wicked and folly, rightly naming it as evil. Yet his concern centers on the honor of his male guest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the host’s words as acknowledging the gravity of the crime (compare 2 Samuel 13:12, where folly names sexual violence). Readers in both traditions commonly recognize his protest as right in what it condemns but tragically limited in whom it protects.

verses.text: Behold, here is my virgin daughter and his concubine. I will bring them out now. Humble them, and do with them what seems good to you; but to this man don’t do any such folly.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the host offering his own daughter and the concubine as a shocking betrayal of those who were most vulnerable in his house. The narrator records it without approval, and readers should not excuse it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the offer as gravely wrong, echoing Lot’s offer in Genesis 19:8. Both traditions commonly read the verse as exposing a moral world in which women’s lives were treated as expendable, a world Scripture here holds up for judgment.

verses.text: But the men wouldn’t listen to him; so the man grabbed his concubine, and brought her out to them; and they had sex with her, and abused her all night until the morning. When the day began to dawn, they let her go.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levite forcing his concubine out to the men, who rape and abuse her through the night. The text states the crime plainly, and the Levite bears real responsibility for handing her over.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise name this as grievous sin by the men of Gibeah and a profound failure by the Levite. Readers in both traditions commonly honor the woman as a victim whose suffering God sees (compare Psalm 10:14), without softening what was done to her.

verses.text: Then the woman came in the dawning of the day, and fell down at the door of the man’s house where her lord was, until it was light.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the woman returning at dawn and falling at the door of the house where her lord was. The image of her at the threshold is quietly devastating.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrator focusing on her suffering, set against the safety of those inside. Both traditions commonly read the verse as calling for grief over what she endured and for justice that the story will show is badly misdirected.

verses.text: Her lord rose up in the morning and opened the doors of the house, and went out to go his way; and behold, the woman his concubine had fallen down at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Levite rises and opens the door intending to go on his way, and only then finds her with her hands on the threshold. His callousness is part of the narrator’s indictment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast between his plan to depart and her position at the door as exposing his lack of care. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as judging the Levite, not commending him.

verses.text: He said to her, “Get up, and let’s get going!” but no one answered. Then he took her up on the donkey; and the man rose up, and went to his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levite’s curt command to get up, and the silence that follows. The text does not say exactly when she died, and readers do well not to speculate beyond it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the stark silence that marks her death or near-death. Both traditions commonly see the verse as one of the most sorrowful in Scripture, and they treat it with restraint rather than elaboration.

verses.text: When he had come into his house, he took a knife and cut up his concubine, and divided her, limb by limb, into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout all the borders of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levite dividing her body and sending it throughout Israel as a shocking act meant to summon the tribes. It compounds the violence done to her rather than honoring her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the act later finds an echo in Saul’s summons with pieces of oxen (1 Samuel 11:7), though the circumstances differ greatly. Readers in both traditions commonly read the deed as part of the moral collapse the narrator exposes, not as an example.

verses.text: It was so, that all who saw it said, “Such a deed has not been done or seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt to this day! Consider it, take counsel, and speak.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people’s response, that such a deed had never been seen since the exodus, as recognition of an unprecedented evil. The call to consider, take counsel and speak invites a response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as marking a national crisis that demands justice. Later prophets remember the days of Gibeah as a byword for corruption (Hosea 9:9; 10:9), and both traditions commonly see the passage as calling God’s people to grieve and act rightly.
